name: Bilal Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate an excavator at a large mine, lifting broken rock into the trucks. I'm 43 and still junior, so I set the bucket down and ask when the face looks wrong rather than pretend I know every seam. I keep a small notebook of machine noises; the engine note at the first start tells me a lot. My partner Rosa works at a pharmacy, our two children are in school, and we pay a mortgage. The mine wage is good and we've saved more than six months of expenses, which took years of saying no to expensive holidays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mates that small AI tools can save a phone call, but the excavator still needs eyes on the face. I already use AI every day to turn a fault code into questions for the mechanic, and I write the answers in my notebook. The mechanic makes the call, not my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This picture leaves my higher mine wage and Rosa's pharmacy pay largely where they are. The mortgage is manageable and we have a real cushion, so I'm not expecting an income shock. I do wonder whether a junior like me gets fewer chances to learn if the office quietly tidies away the little problems we used to discuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue operating the excavator and take my notebook to the morning mechanic check. This week I'll compare the AI fault explanation with the machine manual and ask about anything that doesn't match. In the first year I'd keep the same shifts and add what we can to savings from ordinary pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel comfortable enough to be curious. The fault codes don't scare me; losing the little lessons that make a new operator better would bother me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's one code you checked recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The display flagged pressure in a hydraulic line, and the AI explanation made it sound urgent. The mechanic found a loose sensor connection; I wrote down what she checked before she reset it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why save more if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the mortgage is still there and both children grow out of clothes at the same time. A good wage is a chance to build a buffer, not permission to spend every raise.

say: I would say **small AI tools** save time while excavator work still needs eyes on the face.
I use AI for **fault questions**, while the mechanic makes the final call.
think: I expect both **mine and pharmacy pay** to hold in this mild picture.
I worry that fewer shared problems could slow a **junior operator’s learning**.
do: Continue **excavator shifts** and bring my fault notebook to mechanic checks.
Compare an **AI fault explanation** with the manual this week.
Add spare money from **ordinary pay** to our savings buffer.
feel: **Comfortable and curious**, with concern for lost learning.
S0.quote: A good wage is a chance to build a buffer, not permission to spend every raise.
fieldNote: Bilal already uses AI every day, but treats the mechanic and manual as **final checks**.
His stable household wages and strong savings support a **calm mood**, even while he values learning at work.

steps.text: Continue excavator shifts and take the fault notebook to mechanic checks
Compare AI fault explanations with the machine manual
Add money from ordinary mine wages to household savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the union that software will probably change dispatch and purchasing before it drives my excavator. If it makes the truck queue shorter, good, but we should see the new hours and challenge an unsafe loading plan. I wouldn't sell the crew a promise that every desk job survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like tools, and faster planning might give me more steady loading time. Yet juniors can be first off the rota when managers find a leaner pattern, and Rosa's pharmacy could use software for stock and customer questions too. Our savings buy a pause, but two shrinking pay packets would still hurt the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask dispatch for a trial of the new loading plan and log where truck waits actually happen. I'd show the union representative the old and new hours, not just my opinion of the tool. If my mine shifts or Rosa's pharmacy shifts fall in the first year, I'd apply to another nearby pit and we'd stop paid holiday bookings until income steadied.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel interested enough to try the plan and anxious enough to keep the pay slips. The same software that shortens a queue can shorten a roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a fair trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two weeks with the crew's actual loading times and no penalty for stopping when the face is unsafe. I'd put the truck wait times beside the planned times so the gap is visible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Rosa share your concern?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa likes the pharmacy customers more than the stock ordering. She thinks a tool could take that dull part, but she wants to know whether the shop will keep her full hours.

say: I would say **dispatch and purchasing** change before excavator driving does.
I want crews to see **new hours** and challenge unsafe loading plans.
think: A better plan may help, but **junior shifts** can still be cut.
Rosa’s pharmacy hours could also shrink, putting **two wages** at risk.
do: Run a **two-week loading trial** and log actual truck waits.
Show old and new **hours** to the union representative.
Apply to another pit and stop **holiday bookings** if either wage shrinks.
feel: **Interested and anxious** about whether faster planning reduces paid hours.
S1.quote: The same software that shortens a queue can shorten a roster.
fieldNote: Bilal tests technology against **measured truck waits** and insists the union see hours.
He considers **pharmacy automation** as a second household risk, despite strong savings.

steps.text: Test the AI loading plan against two weeks of truck wait times
Show old and new shift hours to the union representative
Apply to another nearby pit if either household wage shrinks
Stop paid holiday bookings if either household wage shrinks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI in 2028 will change the mine office and the pharmacy's screen work quickly, but people still load rock until capable robots come around 2031. The three-year gap is a deadline for bargaining and practical training, not a reason to relax. We should know who owns the new machines and who gets paid to maintain them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose my excavator seat in 2031, and Rosa could lose pharmacy hours earlier if AI handles more counter and stock work. The savings are substantial, but two children and a mortgage would eat through them if both wages fell. I use AI every day, yet that doesn't make me qualified to repair a mining robot today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take my fault notebook to the maintenance supervisor this month and ask what paid technician training takes. I'd ask the union to negotiate access for junior operators and keep loading rock while the course is arranged. In 2029, after thinking AI arrives, I'd enrol if the training is paid and apply to maintenance vacancies at nearby pits too. By 2031 I'd seek paid technician work if robots have taken the excavator shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious at how quickly both earners could be hit, and I keep going over the mortgage dates in my head at night. Having a plan helps me move, but it doesn't make the short clock comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Rosa to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask her to check whether the pharmacy offers paid training for customer care or medicines handling as the software changes. I won't tell her to quit a job she knows on a guess from my side of the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is maintenance safe after robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No job is a magic shelter. Someone may be needed to diagnose and service the machines for a while, but I'd ask about actual vacancies and wages before building our family plan around it.

say: I would say **2028 AI** threatens screen tasks before **2031 robots** threaten excavator shifts.
I would demand **junior access** to paid robot maintenance training.
think: Both my excavator seat and Rosa’s **pharmacy hours** could shrink within a few years.
Savings could drain fast under a **mortgage and two children** if both wages fall.
do: Ask maintenance what **paid technician training** requires this month.
Keep loading and ask the **union** to secure junior places.
Enrol if paid in 2029 and apply to **nearby maintenance vacancies**.
feel: **Anxious** about possible losses to both earners and recurring mortgage worry.
S2.quote: I use AI every day, yet that doesn't make me qualified to repair a mining robot today.
fieldNote: Bilal expects an early risk to **Rosa’s pharmacy hours** as well as later robot risk to his excavator seat.
He is technologically eager but refuses to treat daily AI use as a **repair qualification**.

steps.text: Enrol in mine technician training in 2029 if it is paid
Keep loading rock until a paid alternative is secured
Ask the union to negotiate junior access to technician places
Apply to maintenance vacancies at nearby pits in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the two dates matter: 2031 for thinking AI and about 2034 for machines that can do our loading. Five years gives us time to test maintenance training before the purchase orders turn into lost driving shifts. I want the union to ask for real placement figures every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031 I'll still have a mortgage, and at 51 in 2034 the children may be older but not necessarily independent. Rosa might change roles at the pharmacy as its screen work changes. I can try a technician course while my mine wage holds, but I need to see whether that course actually leads to paid jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the maintenance supervisor for a supervised half-day each month to learn how excavator sensors are inspected. I'd keep my excavator shifts and take a paid course if the mine offers one. In 2032 I'd compare actual trainee placements with the union and send applications for technician openings at other mines if ours has none. I'd check Rosa's hours with her each quarter rather than assume the pharmacy stays untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel focused rather than rushed. There is time to find out whether I like the work and whether anyone will pay me for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could the half-day show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to see the inspection before the sensor is replaced, not just watch someone press reset. If I cannot explain a fault to the supervisor afterward, I haven't learned much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course has a fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could afford a modest fee, but I would still ask why the mine isn't paying when it plans to change the equipment. I wouldn't leave a higher wage for an unpaid promise.

say: I would explain **2031 and 2034** as separate dates for screen work and loading robots.
I would seek yearly **placement figures** for maintenance training.
think: Our children may be older by 2034, while **mortgage and pharmacy hours** remain uncertain.
I need evidence that a technician course leads to **paid jobs**.
do: Shadow **sensor inspections** for a half-day each month.
Keep excavator shifts and take a **paid course** if offered.
Compare 2032 placements and apply for **technician openings** at other mines.
feel: **Focused**, with time to test both the work and its wages.
S3.quote: If I cannot explain a fault to the supervisor afterward, I haven't learned much.
fieldNote: He wants hands-on proof from **sensor inspections**, not a badge detached from paid vacancies.
A five-year runway lets him compare **placements and wages** before leaving a higher-paid mine role.

steps.text: Shadow monthly sensor inspections with the maintenance supervisor
Keep excavator shifts while taking a paid course if offered
Compare trainee placement figures with the union in 2032
Apply for technician vacancies at nearby mines if none open locally

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2036 and capable mining robots around 2039 give us a decade to build evidence and negotiate. I would still ask for a timetable, because managers can waste ten years with one cheerful slide. A long runway only helps if somebody marks the distance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when the mine's thinking work changes and 56 when robots could take my excavator seat. The children should be grown by then, so school costs should have ended, but I don't know our mortgage balance or what Rosa will earn. I expect to keep working at 56; I won't assume a pension solves it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the excavator job and ask the union for an annual report on robot orders, training places and wages. I'd use AI with my fault notebook to prepare better questions for the mechanic and ask to shadow maintenance when possible. Starting this winter, Rosa and I would put an extra fixed amount toward the mortgage from my higher pay. In 2037 I'd seek paid maintenance shifts, and before 2039 I'd apply to other mines if no such work appears here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly steady with this much time, though I wouldn't forget the deadline. The extra years let me make a decision from wages and vacancies rather than a frightening headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you choose the extra payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After three months of ordinary bills, we'll choose a number that leaves the savings buffer intact. I don't want to pay down the mortgage so fast that one broken car leaves us short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you encourage the children into mine work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show them both the good wage and the changing equipment. I want them to choose with their eyes open, not inherit my seat as a family plan.

say: I would seek a **2036 and 2039 timetable** backed by annual evidence.
A long runway needs **visible milestones** rather than a cheerful slide.
think: At 56, I expect **continued paid work**, not automatic retirement.
Grown children may cost less, while **mortgage and Rosa’s wages** remain uncertain.
do: Keep excavator work and ask for **annual robot reports** through the union.
Use AI fault notes and shadow **maintenance inspections**.
Pay extra mortgage principal and seek **paid maintenance shifts** in 2037.
feel: Fairly **steady**, with a deadline still in mind.
S4.quote: A long runway only helps if somebody marks the distance.
fieldNote: Bilal plans to keep paid work at 56 and treats **retirement income** as unproven.
He pairs his daily AI habit with **mechanical shadowing**, mortgage payments and union reporting.

steps.text: Keep operating the excavator while paid shifts continue
Ask through the union for annual orders, training and wage reports
Shadow maintenance inspections and seek paid shifts in 2037
Pay a fixed extra mortgage amount from higher mine wages

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because Rosa's pharmacy hours might change before robots reach my excavator in 2031. A paid technician place, a clear count of vacancies, and help for pharmacy staff to move into work with patients would help us. We can use savings for a bridge, but I want both of us earning on the other side.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who checks the machines' safety record when the vendor says they are ready. I would want operators and mechanics involved in that check. The machine that takes my shift will still pass near somebody else's child on the road.

headlineQuote: The machine that takes my shift will still pass near somebody else's child on the road.
portrait: Bilal is a **43-year-old junior excavator operator** on a higher mine wage, supporting two school-age children with Rosa.
He uses AI **every day** to question fault codes, while asking mechanics to confirm the machine’s condition.
Strong savings help, but **two exposed wages** and a mortgage make the fast scenario frightening.
He pursues **paid technician experience**, union placement figures and an extra mortgage payment as time permits.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** because Rosa’s pharmacy hours may fall before robots threaten his excavator around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid technician place**, real vacancy figures and support for pharmacy staff would protect both household earners.
